content: Monerans are organisms that are primarily bacteria and other microscopic, single-celled entities. These organisms lack a defined nucleus, meaning their genetic material is not enclosed within a nuclear membrane. In contrast, plants, animals, and other eukaryotic organisms possess a true nucleus where their genetic material is contained. Historically, Monera was considered one of the five biological kingdoms, but modern understanding has reclassified these organisms into two distinct domains: Bacteria and Archaea. This reclassification is based on molecular studies of DNA and RNA sequences, which revealed that Bacteria and Archaea are not closely related to each other and are as distinct from one another as they are from eukaryotes. Consequently, the Monera kingdom has been abandoned in favor of a six-kingdom system and a three-domain system, which treats Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya as separate domains or kingdoms. Before the five-kingdom model, organisms now classified as Monera were divided into two groups within the plant kingdom: Schizomycetes, which were considered fungi, and Cyanophyta, which were thought to be blue-green algae. However, Cyanophyta are now recognized as cyanobacteria, a type of bacteria, and are not closely related to plants, fungi, or animals. Carl Woese, through molecular phylogenetic studies, proposed dividing prokaryotes (formerly Monerans) into two groups: Bacteria and Archaea. His 1990 phylogenetic model, which is rooted in a universal common ancestor, remains widely accepted today. The most modern interpretation of this classification is the Universal and Eukaryote Phylogenetic Tree, which is based on 16S rDNA analysis and is presented in the Tree of Life Web Project. Eubacteria (commonly referred to as Bacteria) and Archaebacteria (now called Archaea) differ significantly in the environments they inhabit. Eubacteria include the majority of bacteria that interact with humans, such as Escherichia coli and Salmonella species. In contrast, Archaea thrive in extreme environments, such as acidic hot springs or deep beneath Arctic ice. The renaming of these groups to Bacteria and Archaea has caused some confusion, as the term bacteria is often used colloquially to refer to all prokaryotic microorganisms, which were historically grouped under Monera. Historically, organisms were classified into three categories: animal, vegetable, or mineral, as outlined in Systema Naturae. The advent of microscopy led to efforts to classify microscopic organisms within either the plant or animal kingdoms. In 1866, Ernst Haeckel proposed a three-kingdom system, introducing Protista as a new kingdom for most microscopic organisms. Within Protista, he included a subgroup called Moneres, which encompassed bacterial groups such as Vibrio. However, Haeckel's Protista kingdom also included eukaryotic organisms now classified as protists. Over time, it became evident that Protista was too diverse to be considered a single kingdom. In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed a five-kingdom classification system, which placed most single-celled organisms into either the prokaryotic Monera or the eukaryotic Protista. The other three kingdoms in his system were the eukaryotic Fungi, Animalia, and Plantae.
